site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Blackie Brings Silver Home
stories.source: Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1912) — Project Gutenberg #62514, Story XVI
body: In a quiet Indian village, the children called the kind old woman Granny, and they doted on the baby Elephant she was given, whom they named Blackie. He grew up swinging little ones on his trunk, visiting Granny each day, and doing no work at all, his days full of gentle play beneath the warm sun.

One morning Blackie noticed how tired Granny had become, and his big heart told him he must help. He walked down to the river where a man struggled to haul heavy wagons through the shallows, and with steady strength Blackie drew each one across, agreeing on two pieces of silver for his labor. When the man tried to cheat him with only one coin per wagon, Blackie planted himself firmly in the road and would not budge until the full bag was counted out and tied around his neck.

Blackie raced home and laid the silver purse at Granny's feet, his eyes soft with love. From that day forward he did all the hard work of the village, Granny rested easy in her chair, and the devoted Elephant and his old friend lived contentedly together, their bond a quiet testament to compassion rewarded.

stories.title: The Elephant Who Remembered Kindness
stories.source: Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1912) — Project Gutenberg #62514, Story XIV
body: By a forest river, carpenters found a great Elephant limping on three feet, a splinter deep in his pad. They knelt in the mud and pulled it free, washing the wound until he could walk again. From that day, the grateful Elephant stayed beside them, hauling trees, rolling logs to the water, and carrying their tools between the sawpits.

In time a beautiful white son joined him, and the two worked trunk to trunk while the carpenters' children splashed and climbed upon their broad backs at the river's edge. One morning the king came down the stream and saw the shining white Elephant at his labour, and he paid a price so great the humble woodcutters wept with thanks.

The young Elephant bade farewell to his playmates and followed the king to the palace, where he was honoured and cared for all his days. The kindness of simple carpenters by the river was repaid a hundredfold, and the king's household was made brighter by a humble forest friendship that none of them ever forgot.

stories.title: Red-Face's Quick Bright Heart
body: On the warm seashore, a rose-apple tree sheltered Red-Face the monkey, and each day his friend Ugly-Mug the crocodile rose from the waves to share fruit and easy talk beneath the leaves. Their friendship sweetened the coast for both of them, a small daily ritual of kindness between sea and shore.

But Ugly-Mug's wife, hungry for the sweetness she tasted on her husband's tongue, demanded he bring her the monkey's heart. So Ugly-Mug coaxed Red-Face onto his back to cross the ocean, and midway confessed the cruel plan. In that dangerous moment, Red-Face stayed calm and answered that his heart still hung in a hollow of the rose-apple tree at home.

The crocodile turned back toward the shore, and as soon as the roots appeared, Red-Face leapt into his tree and vanished among the blossoms, laughing at the trick that saved his life. Wise presence of mind, born of clear thinking when it mattered most, carried him safely home.

stories.title: A Bow, A Bride, A Blessing
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Bala Kanda (Gita Press translation)
body: In the splendid court of King Janaka at Mithila, great rulers gathered and failed, for none could even stir the immense bow of Shiva set as the test for Princess Sita's hand. When Sage Vishvamitra brought Rama forward, the prince bowed with reverence, lifted the heavy weapon, and strung it with ease. As he drew the string, the bow shattered with a thunderous sound, and joy rippled through the hall.

Janaka, his heart overflowing, sent word to King Dasharatha in Ayodhya, and soon the two royal families united in celebration at Mithila. Rama wed gentle Sita, while Lakshmana, Bharata, and Shatrughna married her sisters and cousins, weaving the two houses into one. Blessings were spoken, lamps were lit, and the city glowed with the warmth of an answered prayer.
So began the shared life of Rama and Sita, their path lit by devotion, courage, and the quiet hope that patient hearts will one day find the home they were always meant to share.

stories.title: Savitri Walks with Yama
body: King Ashwapati’s daughter Savitri chose Satyavan as her husband even after the sage Narada warned her that he was fated to die within a year. She married him in the forest hermitage where the blind, exiled king Dyumatsena lived, and quietly counted each passing day.

When Satyavan finally fell at the wood’s edge, Yama himself came to claim his soul. Savitri rose and followed the god of death as he carried Satyavan south, and along the path she praised dharma with such steadfast devotion that Yama offered her boon after shining boon.

At last she asked only that Satyavan’s life be restored. Yama granted it, and Satyavan woke beside her. Dyumatsena’s sight returned, and the exiled royal family journeyed home to reclaim their kingdom, their love proved stronger than fate.
